claims.text: The baseline material is a conventionally cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase lamellar FCC/B2 microstructure.
The baseline alloy has brittle interlamellar interfaces.
Interlamellar interfaces initiate microcracks during room-temperature tensile deformation.
A minor dopant selected for interfacial segregation will segregate to internal interfaces during solidification.
Dopant segregation will modify the chemistry of lamellar colony boundaries.
The modified interfaces will form tougher and more ductile interfacial layers.
Preferential dopant segregation will alter local bonding and phase chemistry at interlamellar interfaces.
Altered local bonding and phase chemistry will inhibit microcrack nucleation and propagation.
Suppression of interfacial brittleness will improve load transfer between the FCC and B2 phases.
Improved load transfer will increase both tensile strength and room-temperature ductility.
The dopant-modified alloy will have higher tensile strength than the unmodified baseline.
The dopant-modified alloy will have substantially greater elongation than the unmodified baseline at room temperature.
The beneficial outcome requires effective dopant segregation without formation of deleterious secondary phases.
Excessive dopant levels or processing conditions that prevent segregation may eliminate the improvements.
The unmodified lamellar-colony baseline exhibits a typical strength-ductility trade-off.

contradictions.description: The targeted interface shifts between lamellar-colony interfaces or boundaries and interlamellar FCC/B2 interfaces. These are distinct microstructural features unless explicitly shown to coincide.
